title: Review: Springs and Hooke's law; Stress, strain and Young modulus; Elastic strain energy
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: D06-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; MT01-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; D06-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; MT01-1#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: D06-1#N.12, MT01-1#N.9, MT03-1#N.11, D06-1#N.2b, MT01-1#N.6, MT03-1#N.4, MT03-1#N.8, MT03-1#N.10. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Extension
items.clue: Stretched length minus the original length, not the whole length.

items.label: Young modulus
items.clue: Gradient of the straight part of a stress–strain graph; about 2 × 10¹¹ Pa for steel.

items.label: Hooke's law
items.clue: Statement that the pull of a spring is proportional to how far it has been stretched.

items.label: Micrometer
items.clue: Instrument used to measure the diameter of the wire in several places and directions.

questions.stem: A spring that obeys Hooke's law is 15.0 cm long when it supports a 3.0 N load and 18.0 cm long when it supports a 6.0 N load. What is its natural (unloaded) length?
questions.explanation: The extra 3.0 N adds 3.0 cm, so the extension is 1.0 cm per newton. With 3.0 N on, the extension is 3.0 cm: natural length = 15.0 − 3.0 = 12.0 cm.

questions.stem: Two cables are made of the same aluminium alloy and carry the same load. Cable Q is 3 times as long as cable P and has 3 times its diameter. Both obey Hooke's law. What is the extension of Q divided by the extension of P?
questions.explanation: Extension = force × length ÷ (area × Young modulus). Same force and material; length × 3; area × 3² = 9. Ratio = 3/9 = 1/3.

questions.stem: A spring obeys Hooke's law. When it is compressed by 3.0 cm it stores 0.45 J. How much energy does it store when it is compressed by 4.5 cm?
questions.explanation: Energy ∝ (compression)². The compression is 1.5 times larger, so E = 0.45 × 1.5² = 1.0 J.

questions.stem: In a lab, a student models a spring as a light spring that obeys Hooke's law. Which statement describes how the spring's force behaves in this model?

options.text: Its force is proportional to its length, measured end to end.
Its force doubles when its extension doubles.
Its force is the same however far it is stretched or compressed.
Its force depends on how fast the attached object is moving.

questions.stem: A student repeats the Young modulus experiment with the same loads on a wire of the same metal and diameter, but only one tenth as long. The extension is read with the same scale. What is the main effect?

options.text: Each extension is ten times smaller, so its percentage uncertainty is ten times larger.
The Young modulus found is ten times smaller.
The stress is ten times larger, so the wire passes its limit of proportionality.
Nothing changes, as the Young modulus is a property of the material.

questions.explanation: Strain is unchanged, so extension ∝ original length. The same reading error is now ten times larger as a fraction of the extension.

questions.stem: A steel wire obeys Hooke's law. A tension of 60 N gives an extension of 1.2 mm. How much elastic strain energy does the wire store?
questions.explanation: Energy = ½ × force × extension = ½ × 60 × 1.2 × 10⁻³ = 0.036 J.

questions.stem: The spring in a toy dart launcher has a spring constant of 400 N m⁻¹. It is compressed by 0.030 m and then released, firing a dart of mass 0.012 kg horizontally. All the elastic potential energy is transferred to the dart's kinetic energy. What is the speed of the dart?

A car's crumple zone is redesigned so that, in the same crash test at the same speed, the front of the car crumples twice as far before the car stops. Assume all the kinetic energy is transferred while the front crumples. What happens to the average force on the car during the crash?

options.text: It doubles, because more of the car is deformed.
It halves, because the same energy is transferred over twice the distance.
It falls to a quarter, because energy depends on the square of the distance.
It stays the same, because the car's kinetic energy is the same.

questions.explanation: Work done = average force × distance = Ek. Ek is unchanged, so doubling the distance halves the average force.
